name: Esther Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good evening, Esther, and thanks for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hartley and Sons, a family firm out in the villages. We repair old farm buildings and barns, and the odd chapel roof, mostly oak frames and lime mortar, nothing modern. Mr Hartley's son Owen picks me up at the crossroads at half seven and we're on site by eight. Today I spent most of it pulling rotten rafters off a cart shed and stacking the good timber to reuse. I love the smell of old oak and knowing the building was up before my great-grandparents were born.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's hard about it, or the money side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still learning the joints, the pegged ones, and I'm slow, so Mr Hartley mostly has me on the heavy work and clearing up. The pay's not much, and winter's thin when the weather stops us. I'm engaged to Mark, he's a mechanic at the garage in Westbury, and we're getting married at St Anne's next June. We've got less than a month's money saved, because most of it's going on the wedding. I don't use any AI things. I've got a phone for calls and the weather and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, good. That's how I'd want it, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and there's no machine that can understand an oak frame that's been standing four hundred years. I'd say it at church, at the pub quiz, wherever. I don't go online, so not there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I'm only just getting started, and I want to learn the trade the way Mr Hartley learned it from his father. If nothing changes, that's still possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, learn the joints, and try and get Mr Hartley to put me through the heritage carpentry certificate at the college. We'd go ahead with the wedding in June as planned, and after that I'd try and save properly, maybe fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want to learn the way Mr Hartley did. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Standing next to him and watching. He doesn't explain much, he just does it, and then hands me the chisel. It's slow, but I remember things better that way than from a book or a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything worrying you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual. Mr Hartley's getting on, and if he stops, Owen's not sure he'll keep the business going. And the wedding costs, that's keeping me up more than anything to do with computers.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, and there's no machine that can understand an oak frame that's been standing four hundred years. I'd say it at church and at the pub quiz.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I'm only just starting and I want to learn the trade the way Mr Hartley learned it from his father. If nothing changes, that's still possible.
S0.do: Carries on as she is, learning the joints, and asks her employer to put her through the heritage carpentry certificate. Goes ahead with the June wedding and then tries to save fifty a month.
S0.quote: He doesn't explain much, he just does it, and then hands me the chisel.
S0.fieldNote: Esther loves the old-building side of the trade and wants to learn by watching, the traditional way. Her worries are her employer's age and wedding costs, not technology. She never uses AI and has no interest in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one's a bit more real, isn't it. You hear about it on the radio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be able to get on with work without being pushed around by big tech firms. Let the market sort it out, but don't let a handful of companies decide everything. And keep the apprenticeships going, that's how people learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right for a while, because nobody's going to send a robot to fix a crooked barn on a hill. But the big building firms might come into our work if their own work dries up. That worries me more than the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Mr Hartley and wait to see what actually happens round here. I'm not going to rush out and learn computers. Maybe I'd hold off on the honeymoon, a week in Cornwall, and put that money aside instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a bit of a draught you can't find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't rush out to learn computers. What if Mr Hartley asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wouldn't. He still does his quotes on a notepad. If Owen took over, maybe. I'd do it if I had to, for the job, but I'd hate it, and I'd be slow. Owen would probably just do it himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Mark talk about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we can still afford the house we wanted in a few years. His work's changing too, cars are all computers now. He's better with it than me. He'd say we'll be fine, and I'd want to believe him.

S1.say: People should be able to work without being pushed around by big tech firms. Let the market sort it out, but don't let a handful of companies decide everything, and keep the apprenticeships going.
S1.think: We'd be all right for a while, because nobody sends a robot to fix a crooked barn on a hill. What worries me more is the big building firms moving into our work if theirs dries up.
S1.do: Keeps working for Mr Hartley and waits to see what happens locally rather than learning computers. Considers cancelling the week's honeymoon in Cornwall and saving that money instead.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a draught she can't find.
S1.quote: Nobody's going to send a robot to fix a crooked barn on a hill.
S1.fieldNote: Esther trusts markets but distrusts big tech, and blames concentration of power rather than the technology. Her private fear is competition from big builders rather than machines. She'd sacrifice the honeymoon before changing how she works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Lord. That's before the wedding's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and the people doing it should answer for it. I'd say families and communities need protecting, not just shareholders. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at church, and I'd sign whatever the vicar put round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the job. Mr Hartley's work would dry up if the big firms can send robots anywhere, even barns. And with less than a month of money and a wedding, there's nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mark about putting the wedding off, or making it small, just the registry and a meal at his parents'. I'd cut everything, no spending on anything but essentials. And I'd lean on family, my parents have a farm cottage that's empty, we'd probably move in there if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not sleeping. Like the ground's gone soft under the scaffold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about any other kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what. I left school at fifteen. I've done the farm, a bit of shop work and this. If there's no work for hands, I don't know where I'd go. I'd pray about it, honestly, that's what I'd do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make the wedding small. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, but it's the marriage that matters, not the party. My nan got married in her work clothes in the war. If it came to it, I'd do the same and not complain. Well, maybe complain a little.

S2.say: It's wrong, and the people doing it should answer for it. Families and communities need protecting, not just shareholders, and I'd sign whatever the vicar put round.
S2.think: I'd lose the job, because Mr Hartley's work would dry up if big firms can send robots anywhere, even to barns. With less than a month of money and a wedding, there's nothing to fall back on.
S2.do: Talks with Mark about postponing the wedding or making it a small registry ceremony. Cuts spending to essentials only and plans to move into her parents' empty farm cottage if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened and not sleeping, as if the ground has gone soft under the scaffold.
S2.quote: My nan got married in her work clothes in the war. If it came to it, I'd do the same and not complain.
S2.fieldNote: Esther falls back on faith, family and community rather than government or retraining. She can't think of other work and says so plainly. The wedding is where the fast picture bites hardest, and she'd make it small without much fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing space, I suppose. I'd be married by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to protect apprenticeships and small firms, before the big ones swallow everything. And let families plan, give people a bit of warning in writing. I'd say it plainly, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be scared, just slower. Five years is enough to get my certificate and maybe get good. But if the end is robots doing hands-on work anyway, I'd have spent five years getting good at something that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hartley to put me through the certificate straight away. We'd go ahead with the wedding but keep it small, and put the rest into savings. And I'd talk to my dad about whether there's a way to make the farm pay something, eggs, holiday lets, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still bad. Lying awake some nights. A bit less than with two years, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't use AI tools. Would you start, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'd rather get very good at the old stuff, the stuff that needs a person who cares. Maybe there's rich people who'll still pay a human for a proper oak frame. I'd bet on that over a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned holiday lets on the farm. Isn't that a big change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and it's not really mine, it's Dad's. But family helps family. If the work goes, the land's still there. That's the one thing a robot can't take off us.

S3.say: This is the time to protect apprenticeships and small firms before the big ones swallow everything, and to give families warning in writing so they can plan.
S3.think: I'd still be scared, just slower. Five years is enough to get my certificate and get good, but if robots take hands-on work at the end, I'd have spent five years getting good at something that goes.
S3.do: Asks Mr Hartley to put her through the certificate straight away. Keeps the wedding small and saves the rest, and talks with her father about earning from the family farm through eggs or holiday lets.
S3.feel: Still frightened and sometimes lying awake, only a little less than with two years.
S3.quote: If the work goes, the land's still there. That's the one thing a robot can't take off us.
S3.fieldNote: Five years barely eases Esther's fear; she sees it as more time to master a skill that will vanish. She still refuses AI tools and bets on wealthy clients paying for handmade oak frames. The family farm becomes her real fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. We might have children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it properly, so do it properly. Keep the apprenticeships, protect family firms, let people earn their way. I don't want handouts, I want there to still be work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like a working life I can actually have. I'd get good, maybe even take over some of Mr Hartley's jobs. The end is still the end, but it's far enough off that I can live in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Mr Hartley, get the certificate in the next two years, and save steadily, fifty or a hundred a month once the wedding's paid off. We'd still try for children, maybe in three or four years. I wouldn't change much else, I'd keep my head down and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, at the back of my mind, but I'd sleep. It's more of a weight than a fright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try for children. Would this picture change when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I'd want them while there's still steady work, so maybe sooner rather than later. Mark wants to wait till we've a house. We'd have to talk about it, and probably pray about it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you ever think about another kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe by the end, if Mr Hartley's gone and the firm's closed. Something with old people, maybe, or the church. But I'd rather not think about that yet. I've only just started this.

S4.say: There's time to do it properly, so do it properly: keep the apprenticeships, protect family firms and let people earn their way. I don't want handouts, I want there to still be work.
S4.think: Ten years feels like a working life I can actually have. I'd get good and maybe take over some of Mr Hartley's jobs, and the end is far enough off that I can live in the meantime.
S4.do: Keeps working for Mr Hartley, gets the heritage certificate within two years and saves fifty to a hundred a month once the wedding is paid off. Plans to try for children in three or four years.
S4.feel: Worried at the back of her mind but able to sleep; more of a weight than a fright.
S4.quote: I don't want handouts, I want there to still be work.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Esther picture a real working life and keep her head down. She thinks about starting a family while work is steady, though she and Mark differ on timing. She'd only consider other work if pushed, at the very end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. We'd have the wedding, no savings and no work, all in one go. What would help is keeping small family firms going, maybe by making the big companies pay something towards apprenticeships, and family and church looking after each other. I don't want to be on benefits, I want work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old buildings. If everyone's thinking about robots and new houses, who's looking after the barns and chapels that are already here? Somebody's got to love them enough to fix them properly.

headlineQuote: Somebody's got to love them enough to fix them properly.
portrait: Esther Wagner is a 27-year-old junior restoration carpenter with a small family firm repairing oak-framed barns and chapels, engaged to a mechanic with a June wedding planned and less than a month of savings. She is churchgoing, traditional and resistant to change, never uses AI, and wants to learn by watching her employer work. A stall leaves her calm and steady change uneasy, with big builders her real fear. AGI by 2028 alarms her and would shrink the wedding and send her to her parents' farm cottage, and five years scarcely helps; ten years lets her picture a working life and plan for children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the wedding, empty savings and losing her job would all hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping small family firms going, perhaps by making big companies fund apprenticeships, and family and church supporting each other rather than benefits.
